newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Dlr hits buffers, stg suffers rate nerves.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Dlr hits buffers, stg suffers rate nerves.

text.p: The dollar's powerful run on the mark hit the buffers on Tuesday when it fell two pfennigs and the pound was knocked from recent peaks by a wave of uncertainty over the outlook for British interest rates.
European equity markets ended with only modest gains, rattled by an unsteady opening on Wall Street. They had climbed strongly in early trade, with some approaching record levels.
The U.S. currency, which surged to a seven-and-a-half year high of 1.8490 marks at one stage on Monday, fell to 1.8290 marks in late European trade as investors took profits.
Speculation was also growing that German officials might step in to support their ailing currency or switch to a variable rate repo in order to defend the mark.

"It's the end of the month, we've had a huge move in the past two-and-a-half weeks and people are putting a little money in the bank," said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer & Co in New York.

In an interview with the German daily Berliner Zeitung, Rolf Peffekoven, a member of the Council of Economic Advisors, dubbed Germany's "five wise men," said Group of Seven industrialized nations could come to the aid of the mark, which sunk to its lowest level against the dollar.

The dollar, up five percent against the mark in the last three weeks, has prospered at the expense of the mark because of a growing conviction that Europe's planned single currency would be launched with a broad group of countries, making for a weak euro.

Sterling, which shed five pfennigs against the mark on Monday, fell another two-and-a-half pfennigs to 2.9829 marks in late European trade as investors began to adopt a more sober outlook for interest rates, currently standing at 6.75 percent.
Forecasts of increases by year-end of up to 8.0 percent in UK base lending rates, which have fuelled sterling's strong run, are being toned down.

Domestic press commentary has begun hand-wringing about the potential for recession early next year if interest rates and sterling are rammed even higher. Exporter calls for a halt in the currency's recent surge have sharpened.

"What we're seeing is a reassessment of some of the more exaggerated interest rate forecasts and sterling is no longer the one-way bet it once seemed," said Neil Parker, treasury economist at Royal Bank of Scotland.
"Sterling had a fantastic rally, and if you put that into context, yesterday's fall was not quite as dramatic as it looked at first sight," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago.
The sell-off Monday was partly prompted by talk the Bank of England might hold off another rate rise at next week's meeting.
Traders also pointed to thin market conditions, which tend to exaggerate market movements.
The falling pound, making British exports more competitive, helped the London bourse at the start but stocks went on to have a choppy day before closing up 0.3 percent.

The FTSE-100 index was lifted initially by engineering stocks which bounced in response to the pound's fall sharp fall. The gains were eroded by the a negative opening on Wall Street but were clawed back as New York turned positive.

In Frankfurt, floor trade, which ended before New York opened, finished with gains of 0.25 percent, but dealings on the after-hours computerised IBIS index was down 0.5 percent by the close at 4377.7 points.
Technical analysts, however, said Frankfurt's greatest bull run in history is set to continue for the time being, although a healthy consolidation phase is on the cards in the medium term.

"I think that we have generally seen a buying panic. Germany is outperforming... all the European indices, and Standard & Poor's at the moment, all of which has to do with the rise of the dollar, which has risen a bit too much at the moment, so we need a small consolidation," said Volker Bien, chartist at BHF Bank in Frankfurt.
Paris stocks finished slightly higher at 3023.63 points, just below Friday's record close, after a quiet session during which the bourse tracked the dollar's performance.
"It's summer. Volumes are slowing down. The market isn't likely either to boom or collapse between now and the autumn," a portfolio manager said.
CURRENCIES
The dollar was at 1.8290 marks and 117.90 yen compared to 1.8466 and 117.70 in late trading on Monday.
STOCK MARKETS
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index finished up 14 points at 4,876.6.
FRANKFURT - The DAX index ended up 10.53 points in bourse trade at 4,381.69.
PARIS - The CAC-40 closed up 1.43 points at 3,023.63.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was ended at $326.45, compared with Monday's close of $327.50. Silver was down six cents at $4.33.
